opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it took some getting used to. When I first arrived, I was surprised by how many meetings there were in a single day. There'd be a morning sync, then a few smaller working sessions, and often something in the late afternoon or evening to wrap things up. Coming from a setting where I had long uninterrupted stretches to think and build, my calendar suddenly felt chopped into little pieces.

For the first couple of weeks I found it draining. I'd come out of a meeting, sit down to do real work, and twenty minutes later it was time for the next one. I remember feeling like I was spending the whole day talking about work instead of doing it.

But over time I started to see why things were set up that way. The company was moving very fast, and the meetings were how everyone stayed aligned. Decisions got made quickly, problems surfaced early, and nobody went off for a week building the wrong thing. Once I understood that, I changed how I worked. I started protecting a few blocks for deep focus, usually early in the morning or late at night, and treated the meetings as the connective tissue rather than an interruption.

So I'd say it didn't suit me naturally at first, but I adapted. Eventually I even came to appreciate the rhythm. It gave the day a kind of pulse, and you always knew where things stood.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes frequent meetings and adapting to them, but does not mention a 10 a.m. meeting, a prior shift to a later time, or that Kay still considered it too early.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it didn't suit me at all at first. I came from a research background where you'd go three or four days without anyone needing to hear from you, and suddenly there's a standup every morning at nine thirty, a sync with the product team at eleven, and some kind of review in the afternoon. My first week I remember feeling like the actual work was happening in the gaps between meetings, and the gaps were tiny.

What changed my mind was realizing the schedule wasn't really about reporting. It was about how fast the ground shifted under us. We'd decide something on Monday, and by Wednesday a competitor had shipped, or a customer call had reframed the whole problem. The morning meeting was less "what did you do yesterday" and more "has anything made yesterday's plan wrong." Once I saw it that way, I stopped resenting it.

I still pushed back on the afternoon one, though. I argued for turning it into a written update, and to the team's credit they tried it for a month. It mostly worked. So I'd say the cadence suited the company more than it suited me, and I adapted about seventy percent of the way, and they adapted the other thirty.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions a 9:30 a.m. standup and discomfort with the schedule, but does not say the company had shifted the meeting later or that Kay still found a 10 a.m. meeting too early.
